title: The Allowance Module
brief: The team installed the Allowance Module so the operations lead can pay Dave's USDC invoices without the owners signing each one. From now on, USDC leaves the Safe only through that module, and the module does nothing else. Everything else the owners do still needs the co-signer.

tests.label: The Allowance Module pays Dave 800 USDC
The Recovery Module pays Dave 800 USDC
The owners pay Dave 800 USDC, co-signed
The Allowance Module approves Mallory to spend 800 USDC
The owners send 1 ETH to Erin, co-signed
The owners send 1 ETH to Dave, co-signed
The owners send 1 ETH to Dave without the co-signer
The Allowance Module sends 1 ETH to Erin

hints: A module transaction cannot be co-signed, so the co-signer catch-all refuses every module transaction.
Give USDC transfers a rule of their own. Which policy looks at who sent the transaction rather than where the tokens go?
Module Allowlist on sending USDC, with the Allowance Module allowed. It refuses the owners on that rule, and here that is the point.
explain: One rule serves owners and modules alike, so the policy has to tell them apart. The module allowlist passes only transactions from modules on its list: owners and the Recovery Module are refused. It checks who sends, not where the tokens go. Limits on amounts and recipients are the Allowance Module's own job. Everything else falls to the co-signer catch-all, which refuses every module transaction, so the module can do nothing else.
